newsitem.title: USA: San Francisco supervisor proposes stadium bond.
newsitem.headline: San Francisco supervisor proposes stadium bond.

text.p: A San Francisco supervisor said Monday he would introduce legislation calling on the city to contribute $100 million to a new $325 million stadium for the 49ers National League Football team.
Supervisor Amos Brown said the legislation would be introduced to meet statutory requirements that allow the measure to be placed before the voters in a June 3 election.

Under the proposal, the city would issue $100 million of lease-revenue bonds to help pay for stadium construction. The bonds would be backed by revenues from a shopping mall the team intends to build as part of the sports complex.
The San Francisco 49ers would be responsible for the balance of the project costs, along with any cost overruns.
The entire project, which will include a retail and entertainment complex, is projected to create 10,000 jobs and generate from $35 to $40 million in annual tax revenues.
"(San Francisco's) general fund is going to benefit," said Michael Colbruno, a spokesman for the project.
The $325 million stadium would be completed by 2000 and completely operational in 2001, officials said. The stadium will seat 75,000, including 185 to 200 luxury boxes and 10,000 club seats.

City officials said the NFL has guaranteed that by building a new stadium, San Francisco would host the Super Bowl that follows the 2001 season. The Super Bowl would generate more than $300 million in economic activity for San Francisco, triple its initial investment, they said.
But opposition has already emerged to the stadium plan with warnings that the team would benefit at taxpayer expense.
One group, called the Committee to Stop the Giveaway, said in a statement that it was preparing an initiative that would prevent stadium subsidies in San Francisco.

"We will be circulating this initiative as we go about from neighborhood to neighborhood arguing against the latest outrageous attempt by the 49ers to pick the pockets of San Francisco's taxpayers," the committee said.
As currently proposed, the city's $100 million lease-revenue bond issue would only require a simple majority to pass in June, city officials said.
